sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial. It asks if a judge can impose consecutive sentences using only prior convictions without a new jury finding.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to require a jury to find new facts before imposing consecutive sentences.
the opposing side wants the Court to allow judges to impose consecutive sentences based solely on prior convictions.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that consecutive sentences require a new jury finding of fact under the Sixth Amendment.
the opposing side argues that prior convictions are sufficient to justify consecutive sentences without a new jury finding.

Chief Justice Roberts asked if enhanced sentences for prior convictions violate Blakely principles.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the limits of judicial sentencing power. It determines whether judges can rely on prior convictions to increase sentences. The outcome shapes the balance between judicial discretion and jury rights in criminal sentencing.
